title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi: a fire the night before, and colors in the morning. Your line was everyone's the same color today. Did you greet someone you'd usually pass? Today, a night nobody sleeps. Day eighty-three.

This festival happens in the dark. Once a year, on the fourteenth night of the waning moon, just before the new moon, in late winter, Shiva temples stay open all night. The lines go around the block. People carry small brass pots of water and milk. They've been fasting since morning. They're not going to bed. Inside, the sound doesn't stop: a bell, a chant, Om Namah Shivaya, again and again, until the sky starts to go gray. It's called Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. And one story people tell about it is about a man who stayed awake by accident.
screen: `A FESTIVAL IN THE DARK.` → `TEMPLES OPEN ALL NIGHT.` → `A MAN AWAKE BY ACCIDENT.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Shiva Purana. A hunter goes into the forest, catches nothing all day, and night falls. Afraid of wild animals, he climbs a tree to wait for morning. It happens to be a bilva tree, the tree whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva. And at its foot, hidden in the dark, is a Shiva lingam, the smooth rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples. The hunter has no idea. All night, to stay awake and keep watch, he shifts and fidgets, and leaves drop from the branches onto the stone below. Water spills from his flask onto it. He hasn't eaten. He doesn't sleep. By dawn, without meaning to, he has done everything this night asks: fasted, kept awake, offered water and bilva leaves to Shiva. In the tellings, when deer come by he lets them go, and his heart changes. And Shiva frees him. Think about what that says. The hunter's intention wasn't holy. He was just scared and stuck in a tree. But he stayed. So that's what people do on Shivaratri. Ratri means night. They fast, they keep a vigil through the night's four watches, and they pour water, milk or honey over the lingam, an offering called abhisheka, and lay bilva leaves on top. Different families remember different reasons for the night. Some say it's Shiva's wedding to Parvati. Some say it's when he danced. We'll come back to those. But the practice is the same: don't sleep through it.
screen: `A HUNTER UP A TREE.` · `LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN STONE.` · `HE STAYED, AND THAT WAS ENOUGH.` · `FAST, KEEP WATCH, POUR WATER.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three breaths longer than you want to. Sit, and close your eyes or lower them. Breathe normally and just watch it. At some point, maybe soon, something in you will say: okay, that's enough, I'm done. When that voice comes, don't argue with it. Just take three more breaths. Like the hunter on his branch, not holy, just staying. Then, if there's time left, stay a little more. The bell holds the time.
Shivaratri. The night of Shiva. Once a year, the great one, kept awake until dawn.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. Today, at the moment you'd usually check out of a conversation or a task, stay three breaths longer. Day eighty-three.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water, milk or honey over the Shiva lingam with bilva leaves, and keep a vigil through the night chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.

original.note: Sanskrit: shiva, the kind or auspicious one, and ratri, night.

trapdoor: what you thought: a night for Shiva's devotees to party.
what it means: a fast and a vigil, water poured over the lingam, and nobody sleeping until dawn.
what a scholar hears: the hunter story is told in the Shiva Purana, and it makes a point about practice: even an accidental vigil counts.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Koti Rudra Samhita (the hunter and the Shivaratri vigil)

notes: The hunter story (often named Gurudruha or Lubdhaka) appears in the Shiva Purana (Koti Rudra Samhita) and elsewhere (e.g. the Garuda and Skanda Puranas in variants). Confirm the citation and the details: the water spilling from his flask, sparing the deer.
Date: krishna chaturdashi (14th of the waning half) of Phalguna (purnimanta) / Magha (amanta), usually February or March. Described as 'late winter'. Confirm.
'Four watches' (prahara) of the night vigil: common practice; confirm.
The lingam described as 'the smooth rounded stone that stands for Shiva'. Confirm this is acceptable wording.
Reasons for the night: Shiva and Parvati's wedding, the tandava; the pillar of light (Lingodbhava) is saved for day 90. Confirm.
Review (2026-10-01): removed the unsourced superlative 'the oldest story' and the 'most festivals' / 'almost everyone' claims.
